_comment: Travel zones — the cost of WATER, which a straight line cannot express.
Backlog F1 (F18 folded in). Port Townsend is ~33 mi from home as the crow
flies and about two and a quarter hours away: a ferry, then the Hood Canal
Bridge. Ranking it beside a 33 mi drive to the Cascades is simply wrong.
WHY ZONES AND NOT A CROSSING TEST. The first design drew the line to the
hotspot and asked whether it intersected water. That was prototyped and it
does not work — the straight line from home to Nisqually NWR crosses Puget
Sound while the road (I-5) drives around the south end and crosses nothing.
Any 'does the route cross water' test reports a ferry for every destination
reachable by going AROUND. Zones ask the answerable question instead: is
the destination on a landmass that costs extra to reach FROM WHERE I AM?
Same zone is free, however much water the straight line happens to clip.
WHY NOT A PER-COUNTY TABLE. Island County contains both Whidbey (ferry)
and Camano (a bridge, free), and King County contains both home and Vashon
(ferry). A per-county penalty is wrong in both directions at once.
THE PENALTY RANKS AND LABELS. IT MUST NEVER FILTER. This is decision 5 in
F1 and it is the whole reason this file is safe. Penalised miles belong in
sort keys and on screen; every `<= MAX_MI` inclusion test keeps taking the
raw straight-line distance. A real chase proved it: an Arctic Tern at
Murden Cove on Bainbridge is 17 mi straight-line — inside today's 30 mi
chase cap and 50 km geo feed — but 52 effective miles, which a penalised
35 mi radius would drop. Rarities arrive through the geo feed, so that
would not have ranked the bird lower, it would have hidden it entirely.
The architecture agrees: eBird's geo feed takes `dist=` as a true radius
and has never heard of a ferry, so what is FETCHED is physically a
straight line and can be nothing else.
Shared byte-identical between the report and the app (the parity suite
compares them exactly and cross-checks the two implementations), so a
ferry costs the same in both.
LIMITS, so nobody re-discovers them: the polygons are hand-drawn and
approximate, and a boundary error is silent — it shows up as one town
being mysteriously cheap, so every zone has a fixture naming real places
on both sides of its edge. `minutes` is one scalar per zone pair, but the
true cost depends on which side you leave by (from Kingston this charges
the Seattle boat for a southbound trip that never queues). Sailing
timetables are NOT modelled: a 06:30 boat and a 17:30 boat are very
different. That is deliberate — the goal is stopping Port Townsend
outranking Marymoor on a Tuesday evening, not predicting your arrival.

zones.label: Olympic W coast
zones._why: The outer Pacific coast, reached by driving US-101 south around through Olympia, Aberdeen and Forks - NO FERRY. Split from `olympic` on 2026-08-04 after scripts/zones_geojson.py showed 126 hotspots, including Third Beach, Toleak Point and Destruction Island, being told to catch a boat. Boundary from the DATA, not taste: the peninsula's hotspots are bimodal in longitude with a trough at -123.5 (3 hotspots) between clusters of 80 and 43, and -123.5 is also where US-101 turns from the north shore down the west side. The lat 47.85 edge keeps the north-west ferry corridor - Neah Bay, Forks, Third Beach are all faster via the ferry and Port Angeles - and is about the Hoh River, where the two routes cross over. 47.85, 47.80 and 47.75 all classify the nine named places identically, so this sits in a stable band rather than on a knife-edge.

zones.label: Bainbridge Is.
zones._why: Bainbridge Island, served by the Seattle-Bainbridge boat or by Agate Pass onto north Kitsap and then the Kingston ferry - either way a crossing. Split from `kitsap` on 2026-08-05 after measurement showed Fort Ward (47.580,-122.523) costs 70 min and takes a boat while Manchester (47.578,-122.545), 1.6 km away on the mainland, costs 60 and takes none. The outline follows the island, including Rich Passage on the south side, because no straight cut separates those two points.

zones.label: Kitsap S+W
zones._why: South and west Kitsap - Bremerton, Port Orchard, Silverdale, Illahee, Manchester, Scenic Beach. Reached by driving round the south sound over the Tacoma Narrows bridge, which is a road: measured 35-60 min with NO ferry on the fastest route. These were inheriting the Edmonds-Kingston ferry label from the old single `kitsap` zone.

bands.label: half day
bands._why: 1.65 h each way. The owner's rule is that one to two hours each way is an excursion, but this sat at 3.0 h round trip - 1.5 h each way - which contradicted it: Murden Cove (1.62 h) and Nisqually (1.56 h) both fall inside the stated rule yet read as full days. 3.3 is the largest value that does NOT also swallow Government Meadows (1.66 h), which is separately known to UNDER-read - the model says 1.7 h and the reality is over 2. Raised 2026-08-05 when splitting Bainbridge out of kitsap gave Murden Cove its own measured cost (68 min, not the 60 borrowed from Point No Point) and exposed the boundary the borrowed figure had been hiding.

bands.label: a trip, not a day out
